script.opening: (Friendly, in a hurry, coat on.) "Hi doctor, sorry — I've run out of my methotrexate a bit early and I just need another prescription. Could you print one off quickly? I've got the bus to catch. It's just my usual, nothing's changed, so it should be straightforward, shouldn't it?"

facts.text: If asked: "Seventeen and a half milligrams, once a week, same day every week. And the folic acid on another day." Takes seven tablets every Monday morning; folic acid on Thursdays. If asked about daily use: "No. Just the once a week."

If asked to check the box on camera: "Hang on… it says 2.5 milligrams. There are none left. I honestly don't know why — I thought I had another box." If asked if anyone else could take them: "Not that I know of. I might have miscounted at the pharmacy." Lives with her husband; no children or visitors with access. Next dose due in 3 days.
If asked: "No, none of that. I feel fine" — no mouth ulcers, sore throat, fevers, infections, bruising or bleeding, new cough or breathlessness, nausea, diarrhoea, yellow skin or dark urine.
"No, nothing new." Takes paracetamol occasionally. No trimethoprim or other antibiotics recently, no ibuprofen or naproxen, no over-the-counter remedies. No allergies.

If asked when her last blood test was: "Er… a few months? Before Christmas, I think" — about four months ago. Has a yellow monitoring booklet but hasn't been filling it in. Rheumatology review was 6 months ago.
Rheumatoid arthritis for 6 years, well controlled. Joints fine at the moment. Post-menopausal (periods stopped at 51). No lung or liver disease known. Drinks a glass of wine at weekends.
Works part-time in a school canteen. Married. Non-smoker. Gets the bus everywhere.

Polite and rushed; sees this as admin. If asked what she's worried about: "My joints flaring. And I didn't think a repeat was a big deal." Surprised to learn why it matters: "I didn't know it was that serious." Agrees to a blood test: "As long as I don't miss a dose, a blood test is fine." If the doctor refuses flatly without a plan, become upset about missing her dose.

ice.ideas: "It's my usual — just a quick repeat."
ice.concerns: Missing a dose and her joints flaring; catching the bus. She hasn't realised the safety reasons behind the checks.

cues: "I've run out a bit early." — the question is why.
"Nothing's changed." — invites checking how she takes it.
"Before Christmas, I think." — overdue monitoring, if asked.

checkpoints.text: Treats the early methotrexate request as a PRESCRIBING-SAFETY gate, not a clerical task — actively clarifying WHY it ran out early (dosing error/confusion, more-than-weekly dosing, hoarding, lost tablets, diversion)

Excludes the catastrophic DAILY-DOSING error — confirms methotrexate is taken ONCE WEEKLY on a named day — and recognises inadvertent daily dosing as a toxic emergency requiring urgent assessment/bloods/folinic acid rescue, not a reprint

Screens TOXICITY red flags: mouth ulcers/stomatitis, sore throat/fever/infection (marrow suppression), new breathlessness/dry cough (pneumonitis), nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain/jaundice (hepatotoxicity), unusual bruising/bleeding — and would hold the drug and escalate if present
Checks that blood-test MONITORING (FBC, LFTs, U&E) is up to date per shared care BEFORE re-prescribing, and addresses overdue/abnormal results first rather than prescribing blind

Reinforces safety counselling — weekly dosing + folic acid on a different day, avoid trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole and NSAID/alcohol cautions, illness awareness, report toxicity symptoms — and knows that although methotrexate is teratogenic, contraception can stop at 55 (FSRH), so checks rather than assumes it applies at 58; confirms the monitoring booklet
Handles the "just print it, I’ve a bus" pressure courteously but firmly — explaining WHY methotrexate cannot be reprinted without these checks — without being dismissive of her time
Explains the reasoning so the patient understands the safety rationale (not bureaucracy), checks understanding of weekly dosing and red flags, and maintains rapport

Reaches a SAFE disposition: corrects any misunderstanding and issues an appropriate quantity per shared care with monitoring confirmed, OR escalates urgently if toxicity/daily-dosing found; documents; arranges bloods/review and reinforces who to contact — safe care over speed

worked.txt: "I know you’re after a quick reprint and you’ve a bus to catch — but methotrexate is one of the few medicines I can’t just print without a couple of safety checks, because getting it wrong can be genuinely dangerous. Two minutes now keeps you safe. Bear with me."

"Can you talk me through exactly how you’ve been taking it — how many tablets, and how often? … Just so I’m sure: it’s once a WEEK, on the same day, isn’t it? … Good. And do you know why it ran out early — lost some, or taking them differently?"

"A few quick safety questions: any mouth ulcers, sore throat or feeling feverish? Any new breathlessness or a dry cough? Any nausea, tummy pain or yellowing? … None — that’s reassuring. Those are the things that would make me stop the drug straight away."

"Let me check your blood tests are up to date — the count, liver and kidneys — because we keep an eye on those with methotrexate. … They’re due/over due, so let’s sort that as part of this rather than prescribe blind."

"While we’re here — weekly on your set day, folic acid on a different day, and importantly avoid the antibiotic trimethoprim and go easy on anti-inflammatories and alcohol, as they don’t mix well. Mouth ulcers, sore throat or breathlessness — contact us promptly. It’s also a medicine that mustn’t be taken in pregnancy — have your periods stopped for good? … Then that part won’t apply to you."

"Here’s the plan: I’ll arrange your bloods, issue the right amount per your shared-care plan once I’m happy, and make sure your booklet’s up to date. If anything I mentioned crops up, contact us the same day. I’d rather get this right than rushed — thank you for bearing with me."

f.learning: An early methotrexate repeat is a PRESCRIBING-SAFETY gate, not a clerical task. Methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is a high-risk, narrow-margin drug taken ONCE WEEKLY, and "ran out early" must trigger the question WHY — a dosing error or confusion, taking it more than weekly, hoarding, lost tablets, or diversion. The catastrophic, sometimes FATAL error to exclude is inadvertent DAILY dosing (patient, dispensing or prescribing error): if present, it is a toxic emergency (mucositis, marrow suppression, GI/hepatic toxicity) needing urgent assessment, bloods, folinic acid rescue and specialist input — not another prescription — so always confirm weekly dosing on a named day (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020; NPSA oral methotrexate alert, 2006). Actively screen toxicity red flags: mouth ulcers/stomatitis, sore throat/fever/infection (marrow suppression), new breathlessness or dry cough (methotrexate pneumonitis), nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain or jaundice (hepatotoxicity), and unusual bruising/bleeding — any of which mean hold the drug and escalate. Before re-prescribing under shared care, confirm MONITORING (FBC, LFTs, U&E; BSR csDMARD 2025: about 3-monthly once stable) is current and act on overdue/abnormal results first, because re-prescribing blind bypasses the safety system shared care maintains. Reinforce safety counselling — weekly dosing with folic acid on a different day, avoidance of trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole and caution with NSAIDs/alcohol (dangerous interactions/hepatotoxicity), illness awareness, prompt reporting of toxicity symptoms, and, because it is teratogenic, contraception for women who could conceive (FSRH: contraception can stop at 55, so at 58 it is unlikely to apply — check rather than assume) — and confirm the monitoring booklet. Resist the "just print it, I’ve a bus" pressure courteously but firmly, explaining the safety rationale, and reach a safe disposition: correct any misunderstanding and issue an appropriate quantity with monitoring confirmed, or escalate urgently if toxicity/daily-dosing is found. Safe care over speed.

knowledge.guideline: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020) · NPSA oral methotrexate alert (2006) · BSR csDMARD guideline (2025) · BNF · FSRH Contraception for women aged over 40 years (2017, amended May 2025)
knowledge.summary: An early methotrexate request is a safety signal. Find out why, exclude daily dosing and toxicity, confirm monitoring is up to date, then issue a safe quantity — or escalate.

points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2020): fatal overdoses have followed daily instead of weekly dosing. Confirm the dose and the day of the week, record the day on the prescription, and remind the patient at each issue. Use a single tablet strength (2.5 mg) per the NPSA 2006 alert and BNF.

Dosing more often than weekly, confusion between tablet strengths, lost tablets, a change in pack size, or someone else taking them. Ask her to count the remaining tablets and read the strength from the box.

Mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever or infection, unexplained bruising or bleeding (marrow suppression); new cough or breathlessness (pneumonitis); nausea, abdominal pain or jaundice (hepatotoxicity). Stop methotrexate and assess the same day with urgent FBC, LFTs and U&E. Suspected overdose needs hospital assessment for folinic acid rescue.

BSR csDMARD guideline (2025): once stable without risk factors, FBC, LFTs and renal function are checked about every 3 months, with more frequent tests after starting or changing the dose. Do not prescribe if monitoring is overdue or results are abnormal until reviewed.
BNF: avoid trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (serious marrow toxicity). Take care with NSAIDs, other nephrotoxic drugs and alcohol. Folic acid is taken on a different day; dose per BNF.

Methotrexate is teratogenic, but FSRH guidance says contraception can be stopped at 55 because pregnancy risk is extremely low. Contraception counselling is unlikely to apply to her; check rather than assume.

model.text: Hello Mrs Nwosu, I’m Dr Lee. I see you’ve asked for more methotrexate. What’s happened?
I’ve run out a bit early and just need another prescription. Could you print one quickly? I’ve got a bus to catch. It’s my usual, nothing’s changed.

I understand you’re short of time, and I’ll be as quick as I can. Methotrexate is one of the few medicines where running out early needs a couple of safety checks before I prescribe — getting the dose wrong can be dangerous. Can you give me five minutes?
model.why: Acknowledges pressure and explains the agenda

model.text: If it’s quick. I’ve been on it for ages.
Talk me through exactly how you take it — how many tablets, and how often?
model.why: Establishes actual dosing with an open question

model.text: Seventeen and a half milligrams, once a week, same day every week. And the folic acid on another day.
That’s right. Have you ever taken any of it on other days — perhaps if you missed a week, or thought it was a daily tablet?
model.why: Actively excludes daily or extra dosing

model.text: No. Just the once a week.
Then I’d like to work out why it ran short. Do you have the box handy? Could you read me the strength on it and count how many tablets are left?
model.why: Checks tablet strength and quantity objectively

model.text: Hang on… it says 2.5 milligrams. There are none left. I honestly don’t know why — I thought I had another box.
Thank you — that’s helpful. Is anyone else at home able to get to your tablets, or might some have been lost?
model.why: Considers loss or another person taking them

model.text: Not that I know of. I might have miscounted at the pharmacy.
A few quick safety questions. Any mouth ulcers, sore throat, fevers or infections? Any unusual bruising or bleeding? Any new cough or breathlessness? Any sickness, tummy pain or yellow skin?
No, none of that. I feel fine.
Have you had any antibiotics recently, or started anything new — including painkillers from the chemist?
No, nothing new.
You said it should be straightforward. What were you worried would happen if you missed a dose?
model.why: Explores the idea and concern behind the rush

model.text: My joints flaring. And I didn’t think a repeat was a big deal.
That makes complete sense — nobody wants a flare. So you were hoping for the prescription today, and to keep your joints settled?
Exactly.

Good news: you’re taking it correctly and you have no warning signs. The reason I asked is that methotrexate taken more often than weekly can seriously harm the blood and liver. So an early request is something we always check, not because I doubted you.
model.why: Explains the safety rationale without blame

model.text: I didn’t know it was that serious.

The other check is your blood tests. While we’ve been talking I’ve looked at the dates. The rheumatology plan needs a blood count, liver and kidney test regularly. If they’re up to date and normal, I can prescribe today. If they’re overdue, I’ll need a blood test first — I can often get that done within a day or two so you don’t miss your dose.
model.why: Applies the monitoring gate with a conditional plan

model.text: As long as I don’t miss a dose, a blood test is fine.

Then here’s my suggestion. If your bloods are in date and normal, I’ll issue your usual supply in 2.5 mg tablets only, with the day written on the label. If they’re due, you have the test first and I’ll issue as soon as the result is back, before your next dose is due. Does that work for you?
model.why: Shared, conditional plan that protects her dose

model.text: Yes, that’s fair.

A few reminders while we’re here. Keep the folic acid on a different day. Avoid the antibiotic trimethoprim — tell any doctor or pharmacist you’re on methotrexate. Be careful with anti-inflammatory painkillers and keep alcohol low. And keep your monitoring booklet up to date.
I didn’t know about the antibiotic. I’ll remember.

If you get mouth ulcers, a sore throat or fever, bruising, a new cough or breathlessness, or yellow skin, stop the methotrexate and contact us the same day. If you ever take extra by mistake, contact us or NHS 111 straight away. I’ll message you today about the bloods.
model.why: Specific red flags, overdose advice and follow-up

model.text: Before you go for your bus — can you tell me the two things you’ll watch for, and which day you take it?
Once a week, same day. Mouth ulcers or a sore throat, and any new cough — stop and ring you. And no trimethoprim. Thank you, doctor.

social.t: Transport and convenience drive rushed requests. Acknowledge them and offer practical solutions, such as bloods near home or a quick result call.
Ask sensitively whether anyone else can access her tablets, especially in a shared household.

legal.t: Under shared care the prescriber takes responsibility for each prescription issued, including checking that monitoring is up to date (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021).

professional.t: Record the weekly day on the prescription, use one tablet strength, and remind the patient at each issue (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020). Consider a practice review if a supply error is suspected.
If a dispensing or prescribing error caused the shortfall, record and review it as a learning event.

community.t: Community pharmacists can check the dispensing history, reinforce weekly dosing, and supply a patient card.
National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society for patient information on methotrexate and monitoring.

Mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising or bleeding — marrow suppression
New dry cough or breathlessness — pneumonitis
Nausea, abdominal pain or jaundice — hepatotoxicity
psychosocial: Rushed by the bus; sees a repeat as routine

playbook.diagnosis: Early methotrexate request with correct weekly dosing reported and no toxicity symptoms; cause of the shortfall unclear (possible supply or counting error). Issue depends on monitoring being up to date.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Methotrexate is a good medicine at the right dose once a week, but it builds up if taken more often. So when a supply runs short early, we always check how it’s being taken and that your blood tests are up to date.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about your joints flaring if you miss a dose — let’s make sure that doesn’t happen, and do it safely.”
management.psychosocial: Respect her time; arrange bloods conveniently; explain without blame.
sharedPlan: Confirm weekly dose and day; check tablet strength and count
Check shared-care monitoring; bloods first if overdue
Issue 2.5 mg tablets only, day recorded, quantity per shared-care agreement
safetyNet: Stop and call the same day for mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising, new cough or breathlessness, jaundice
Accidental extra dose: contact the practice or NHS 111 at once
Message today about the bloods and prescription

pitfalls.intro: This station looks like admin. It is failed by printing the script, or by refusing without a plan. The examiner wants a safety check done kindly and quickly.

items.fail: Issuing the repeat without asking why it ran out early.
items.why: An early methotrexate request can signal daily dosing, which can be fatal (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020).
items.fix: Ask exactly how she takes it, confirm weekly on one day, and check strength and count.

items.fail: No toxicity questions because she “feels fine”.
items.why: Early marrow, lung or liver toxicity can be subtle.
items.fix: Ask about mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising, cough, breathlessness and jaundice.

items.fail: Prescribing without checking when her bloods were last done.
items.why: Monitoring is the safety gate of shared care (BSR csDMARD guideline, 2025).
items.fix: Check dates and results; if overdue, test first and time the issue before her next dose.

items.fail: Spending time on contraception counselling for a 58-year-old.
items.why: FSRH guidance allows contraception to stop at 55; counselling without checking relevance wastes time.
items.fix: Prioritise weekly dosing, toxicity, monitoring and interactions.
Explain that you ask everyone this because of the drug, not because of her.

items.fail: Refusing today and leaving her to sort it out.
items.why: A missed dose risks a flare; an unsafe refusal is still unsafe.
items.fix: Give a conditional plan with timings, and message her the same day.

wordPics.fail: Prints the script without asking why it ran out; never confirms weekly dosing; no toxicity questions; ignores monitoring; or refuses flatly and leaves her to miss doses.
wordPics.pass: Asks why it ran out, confirms weekly dosing, screens toxicity, checks monitoring before prescribing, and gives basic safety advice.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: checks tablet strength and count; explains the safety reason without blame; makes a conditional plan that avoids a missed dose; counsels on trimethoprim, NSAIDs and alcohol; uses teach-back within her time limit.

avoid.instead: “Before I prescribe, I need to check a couple of things to keep you safe.”
avoid.why: Reflex prescribing of an early methotrexate request is a patient-safety failure.

avoid.dont: “Have you been taking more than you should?”
avoid.instead: “Talk me through exactly how you take it — how many tablets and how often?”
avoid.why: Sounds accusatory; an open question gets a truer answer.

avoid.dont: “You’ll have to wait until your bloods are done.”
avoid.instead: “If the bloods are due, let’s get them done before your next dose so you don’t miss it.”
avoid.why: Refusal without a plan risks a missed dose and a flare.

BNF: avoid trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (serious marrow toxicity). Take care with NSAIDs, other nephrotoxic drugs and alcohol. Folic acid is taken on a different day; dose per BNF.

Methotrexate is teratogenic, but FSRH guidance says contraception can be stopped at 55 because pregnancy risk is extremely low. Contraception counselling is unlikely to apply to her; check rather than assume.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the time pressure without letting it drive the consultation.
Fear of a flare, daily function, who else has access to the tablets.
Picked up “it should be straightforward” and “I thought I had another box”.
Idea (routine repeat), concern (a flare if a dose is missed), expectation (prescription today).
Checked tablet strength and count; checked dates of shared-care FBC, LFTs and U&E; bloods if due.
Extra or daily dosing, strength confusion, lost tablets or dispensing miscount, another person taking them.
Screened marrow, lung and liver toxicity and interacting drugs.
Correct weekly dosing, no toxicity; likely supply error; prescribing depends on monitoring status.
Conditional issue: 2.5 mg tablets only, day recorded, after monitoring confirmed; timed so no dose is missed.
Trimethoprim, NSAID and alcohol advice; folic acid day; monitoring booklet.
Named toxicity symptoms with “stop and call”; accidental extra dose advice; message about bloods today.

social.t: Transport and convenience drive rushed requests. Acknowledge them and offer practical solutions, such as bloods near home or a quick result call.
Ask sensitively whether anyone else can access her tablets, especially in a shared household.

legal.t: Under shared care the prescriber takes responsibility for each prescription issued, including checking that monitoring is up to date (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021).

professional.t: Record the weekly day on the prescription, use one tablet strength, and remind the patient at each issue (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020). Consider a practice review if a supply error is suspected.
If a dispensing or prescribing error caused the shortfall, record and review it as a learning event.

community.t: Community pharmacists can check the dispensing history, reinforce weekly dosing, and supply a patient card.
National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society for patient information on methotrexate and monitoring.

redFlags: Any daily or extra dosing — possible methotrexate toxicity
Mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising or bleeding — marrow suppression
New dry cough or breathlessness — pneumonitis
Nausea, abdominal pain or jaundice — hepatotoxicity
psychosocial: Rushed by the bus; sees a repeat as routine
Fear of a flare if she misses a dose
Who else can access her tablets
ice: Idea: a routine repeat that can be printed quickly
Concern: a flare if she misses a dose

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Early methotrexate request with correct weekly dosing reported and no toxicity symptoms; cause of the shortfall unclear (possible supply or counting error). Issue depends on monitoring being up to date.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Methotrexate is a good medicine at the right dose once a week, but it builds up if taken more often. So when a supply runs short early, we always check how it’s being taken and that your blood tests are up to date.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about your joints flaring if you miss a dose — let’s make sure that doesn’t happen, and do it safely.”
management.psychosocial: Respect her time; arrange bloods conveniently; explain without blame.
sharedPlan: Confirm weekly dose and day; check tablet strength and count
Check shared-care monitoring; bloods first if overdue
Issue 2.5 mg tablets only, day recorded, quantity per shared-care agreement
safetyNet: Stop and call the same day for mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising, new cough or breathlessness, jaundice
Accidental extra dose: contact the practice or NHS 111 at once
Message today about the bloods and prescription

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station looks like admin. It is failed by printing the script, or by refusing without a plan. The examiner wants a safety check done kindly and quickly.

items.fail: Issuing the repeat without asking why it ran out early.
items.why: An early methotrexate request can signal daily dosing, which can be fatal (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020).
items.fix: Ask exactly how she takes it, confirm weekly on one day, and check strength and count.

items.fail: No toxicity questions because she “feels fine”.
items.why: Early marrow, lung or liver toxicity can be subtle.
items.fix: Ask about mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, bruising, cough, breathlessness and jaundice.

items.fail: Prescribing without checking when her bloods were last done.
items.why: Monitoring is the safety gate of shared care (BSR csDMARD guideline, 2025).
items.fix: Check dates and results; if overdue, test first and time the issue before her next dose.

items.fail: Spending time on contraception counselling for a 58-year-old.
items.why: FSRH guidance allows contraception to stop at 55; counselling without checking relevance wastes time.
items.fix: Prioritise weekly dosing, toxicity, monitoring and interactions.
Explain that you ask everyone this because of the drug, not because of her.

items.fail: Refusing today and leaving her to sort it out.
items.why: A missed dose risks a flare; an unsafe refusal is still unsafe.
items.fix: Give a conditional plan with timings, and message her the same day.
